Q1.text:
Kalshi sports data is a three-level tree: series > event > market. A series is the recurring product. For NFL game winners that is KXNFLGAME (category "Sports", tag "Football", frequency "custom", settlement source "the Governing League"). An event is one game: KXNFLGAME-26OCT01PITCLE, titled "PIT Steelers vs CLE Browns". A market is one yes/no contract inside the game. This game has two: KXNFLGAME-26OCT01PITCLE-PIT ("Pittsburgh") and ...-CLE ("Cleveland"). The event is flagged mutually_exclusive = true, so exactly one of the two pays out. The ticker itself encodes the structure: series, then date (26OCT01), then away+home team codes, then the outcome team.

The links are clean. The app checked every record: the event's series_ticker matched the series (1 of 1), and both markets' event_ticker matched the event (2 of 2). The markets nested inside GET /events/{event_ticker} were identical to the GET /markets list (2 and 2, nothing missing on either side).

The market object is where the useful data lives: 47 fields observed. For a price comparison the important ones are yes_bid_dollars (0.5900), yes_ask_dollars (0.6000) and last_price_dollars (0.6000), plus volume_fp (3,849,232.05 contracts), volume_24h_fp (3,457,505.96), open_interest_fp (3,651,244.11) and status ("active"). Two formatting details matter when we build the dataset. Prices come back as dollar strings with four decimals, and contract counts are fixed-point strings ending in _fp, so both need converting to numbers. Every contract has a $1.00 notional (notional_value_dollars) and trades in 1-cent steps (price_level_structure "linear_cent"), so a YES price of $0.60 reads directly as a 60% implied probability before fees.

The series also carries the fee setup we covered in Task 1: fee_type "quadratic_with_maker_fees" with fee_multiplier 1.

Twelve market fields listed in the spec were not present on this live market, for example settlement_ts and settlement_value_dollars. They only show up once a market settles. No observed field was outside the spec, and no value fell outside a spec enum.

Older games stay in the same structure. Paging GET /events for KXNFLGAME with status=settled returned 429 game events, going back to KXNFLGAME-25JUL31LACDET (the July 31, 2025 preseason opener).

Q2.text:
Each data source carries a different timestamp.

1) Candlesticks use end_period_ts, a Unix-seconds integer marking the END of the period. Hourly and minute candles line up on the clock (offset 0). Daily candles end at 04:00 UTC, not midnight (offset 14,400 s), and the January archived game's daily candle ended at 05:00 UTC. So a Kalshi "day" is midnight-to-midnight Eastern time, and it moves with daylight saving.

2) Trades use created_time, an ISO 8601 UTC string. The number of decimal places varies from trade to trade (we saw 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 fractional digits), so a parser has to accept all of them. Trades are the most precise source. The last 20,000 trades before the game had a median gap of 0.31 seconds, a longest gap of 8.8 seconds, and at least one trade in every one of 173 one-minute buckets.

3) The orderbook has no timestamp field at all (request 893). The only time reference is the HTTP Date header, which is rounded to the whole second.

4) Market metadata timestamps (open_time, close_time, expected_expiration_time, etc.) describe the contract's schedule, not price activity. updated_time on this market still read 2026-09-22T04:05:01Z even though the price was moving every second. The event's last_updated_ts came back as 0001-01-01T00:00:00Z, a placeholder value.

Completeness depends on how busy the market is. Over the 9.8 days, 1-minute candles covered only 7,074 of 14,157 possible minutes (50.0% missing). Kalshi skips minutes with no activity, and 1,916 of the candles returned had no trade price at all. Only 36.4% of minutes had an actual trade. The longest stretch without any candle was 122 minutes. Hourly candles were nearly complete (234 of 236 hours). This matters for our matching. Early in the week there were long quiet periods with no Kalshi price, but in the hours before the game there was a trade almost every second.

The data exists for archived games too. The SF at SEA game (Jan 18, 2026) returned 978 one-minute candles, one for every minute from 12:00 UTC until the market closed, and 10,000 trades from the historical endpoints.

Clocks: comparing the Date header with our local clock gave offsets of -0.3 to -0.9 seconds. That is within the 1-second rounding of the header, so for minute-level matching against sportsbook odds, clock drift is not a concern.

Q3.text:
Kalshi splits data at a cutoff date that GET /historical/cutoff reports. Today it returned trades_created_ts = 2026-08-02 and market_settled_ts = 2026-08-02. Markets settled before that date, and trades created before it, live only under the /historical endpoints. Anything newer is on the regular live endpoints.

The two sides do not overlap. The archive matrix checked the same market against both sets of endpoints:
- Archived game (LA at SEA, settled Jan 27, 2026): GET /markets/{ticker} returned 404 and GET /historical/markets/{ticker} returned 200 (requests 934-935). The live candlestick endpoint returned 404 (request 939).
- Settled after the cutoff (PHI at CHI, Sept 28, 2026): the live market returned 200 and the historical market 404. Live candles returned 24 hourly records; historical candles returned 404 (requests 941-947).
- Tonight's game (PIT at CLE, still active): live only. The historical market and candle endpoints both returned 404.
In practice, any data pull has to check the cutoff first and then choose the endpoint.

How far back it goes, for NFL game markets (KXNFLGAME):
- /historical/markets: 666 markets, settlement dates from 2025-08-01 to 2026-02-15. The walk reached the end of the list, so that is the full archive for this series.
- /markets?status=settled: oldest settlement 2026-08-07, newest 2026-09-29.
- /markets/trades for tonight's market: oldest trade 2026-09-22 06:45 UTC, about 2 hours 40 minutes after the market opened. Newest was a few seconds before the query.
- /events (settled) still lists every game back to the July 31, 2025 preseason opener, even for games whose markets are archived.

The archive keeps minute-level detail. For SF at SEA (Jan 18, 2026, volume 14,304,507 contracts) the historical endpoints returned a 1-minute candle for every minute up to the market close, and 10,000 trades in the last 2.3 hours (we stopped at our page cap, so there are more). So last season's playoff games can be rebuilt at minute level.

One caution. The first archived LA at SEA market we sampled returned zero candles and zero trades for the game window. Its record shows last price $0.00 and open interest 0, so that particular contract never traded. An empty response from /historical can mean the contract never traded, not that the data is gone. Check volume_fp before treating it as missing.

Live-only data: the orderbook. It returns current bids only, with no timestamp and no history endpoint, so past depth cannot be recovered. It has to be recorded live.

Q4.text:
Authentication. Every market-data GET we tested works without a key. The probe called 40 GET endpoints twice, once without our key and once with it. 36 returned 200 with no key, matching the spec. That includes markets, events, series, trades, candlesticks (live and historical), orderbooks and /historical/cutoff. Two needed the key: /account/limits and /account/api_usage_level/volume_progress returned 401 without it and 200 with it (requests 812-815). Two /live_data endpoints returned 404 both ways, so we couldn't classify them. We left the 36 portfolio/account endpoints out of the probe on purpose, since they are personal data and not needed. Four more could not be probed because they need IDs we could not discover. The WebSocket is the exception: auth_notes.md says it needs a signed handshake even for the public ticker and trade channels. Signing is RSA-PSS with SHA-256 over timestamp + method + path, sent in three KALSHI-ACCESS-* headers.

Rate limits. GET /account/limits says our key is on the "basic" tier, with a read bucket that refills at 200 tokens per second up to a capacity of 600. GET /account/endpoint_costs gives a default cost of 10 tokens per request. That works out to about 20 reads per second sustained, or a burst of about 60. This matches the Basic row in rate_limits.md (200 read / 100 write). The ramp test sent 10 requests each at 1, 1.5 and 2 requests per second. All 30 returned 200, with median latency of 75-77 ms and no 429s. None of the 9 response headers were rate-limit headers: no Retry-After and no X-RateLimit-*. The docs say the same, so we cannot see the remaining budget and have to track it ourselves.

Pagination is cursor-based. On /markets/trades: no limit gave 100 rows, limit=1000 (the spec maximum) gave 1,000, and limit=1001 was rejected with HTTP 400 ("failed on the 'lte' tag"). limit=0 did not return zero rows; it fell back to the default 100 (request 1014). Walking 5 pages of 1,000 trades for tonight's market gave 5,000 unique trades with zero duplicates and a 46-character cursor every time. We never reached the end, because this one market had more than 5,000 trades.

What it means for scale. A busy NFL market produced 20,000 trades in under 3 hours on game day. At 1,000 per page that is 20 requests. Even 100 pages would take about 5 seconds at the documented 20 requests per second. Our tool runs much more conservatively at 2 per second, which would take about 50 seconds. Rate limits are not the bottleneck for this project.

Q5.text:
[AI-drafted from Kalshi Recon data collected Oct 1, 2026. Review and edit before submitting.]

Checked Oct 1, 2026 (API v3.32.0). Based on the M1 catalog (117 operations in the spec) and the runs behind Q1-Q4 and Q6.

Most useful for matching a Kalshi price to a sportsbook line at the same minute:

1) Candlesticks: GET /series/{series_ticker}/markets/{ticker}/candlesticks, and GET /historical/markets/{ticker}/candlesticks for archived games. 1-minute, 1-hour and 1-day candles with trade OHLC plus closing yes bid/ask, volume and open interest. This is the most direct way to get "the Kalshi price at minute X". Example: 7,074 one-minute candles for tonight's PIT market, and a complete minute series for the archived SF at SEA game.

2) Trades: GET /markets/trades and GET /historical/trades. Every trade, with created_time to the microsecond, filterable by ticker and min_ts/max_ts. Use these when a minute has no candle, or to check candle prices against actual executions. Tonight's market traded about every 0.3 seconds in the hours before the game.

3) GET /historical/cutoff decides which of the two sets of endpoints to call (live or historical). Without it, requests for older games return 404.

4) Discovery and metadata: GET /search/tags_by_categories and /search/filters_by_sport (to find sports series), GET /series/{series_ticker}, GET /events (lists past games back to July 2025), GET /events/{event_ticker} and GET /markets / GET /markets/{ticker}. These give us team names (yes_sub_title), scheduled times, the rules text, status and the result. We need them to line each Kalshi market up with the matching sportsbook event and outcome.

5) Fees: the series fee_type and fee_multiplier fields, and GET /series/fee_changes. These connect the Task 1 fee model to each market, so we can compare what a consumer actually pays.

6) Live capture: the WebSocket ticker and trade channels (see Q6), only if we record games as they happen.

Useful but limited:
- GET /markets/{ticker}/orderbook and /markets/orderbooks show current depth only, with no timestamp and no history. Good for spread and liquidity snapshots, not for backtesting.
- GET /markets/candlesticks (batch) could pull several markets at once.
- /live_data/milestone/{id}/game_stats returned 200, so game-state data might help align prices with in-game events. The other two /live_data endpoints returned 404 for the IDs we tried, so we haven't confirmed this.

Not useful for our scope: GET /exchange/status, /exchange/schedule and /exchange/user_data_timestamp (exchange housekeeping); /incentive_programs, /structured_targets and /multivariate_event_collections (promotions and parlay-style products, not single-game prices); and all 36 /portfolio and /account endpoints apart from /account/limits. Those cover our own orders, balances and positions.

Q6.text:
What we saw:
- The WebSocket connected once (HTTP 101, request 1021), never dropped, and delivered 7,273 messages: 893 ticker updates and 6,380 trades. Trade sequence numbers ran 1 to 6,380 with no gaps and nothing out of order.
- Price changes: the WebSocket showed the bid/ask/last-price combination changing 77 times. REST polling at 2 seconds caught only 18 changes. In 49 of 449 polling intervals the price moved on the WebSocket but REST saw nothing new, and in 18 intervals the price moved more than once between polls. By the app's count, REST missed 68 changes: a poll can only show where the price ended up, not the moves in between.
- Trades: no difference in what was captured. All 6,370 trades in the comparison window appeared in both feeds (0 WebSocket-only, 0 REST-only). REST just got them later: median 1.06 seconds after the WebSocket, up to 2.4 seconds, which is basically the polling interval.
- Speed: WebSocket messages arrived a median 41 ms after Kalshi queued them (sending_ts_ms). Trade messages arrived 46 ms after the trade time. Ticker messages lagged their own timestamp more (median 181 ms, p95 565 ms), and their arrival times clustered at the same point in each second, which looks like the ticker channel is sent in batches about once a second. A REST request took a median 74 ms.
- Cost: REST used 900 requests in 15 minutes, 1 per second the whole time. The WebSocket used 3 (one handshake and two subscribes). The price moved from 0.59/0.60 to 0.62/0.63 during the window.

Which is better for our scope? It depends which half of the study we are doing.

For historical matching against sportsbook odds (the main study), REST wins by default. The WebSocket only streams from the moment you subscribe and has no replay, so past games can only come from the REST candlestick and trade endpoints (Q3).

For recording games live, the WebSocket is clearly better. It catches every price move, delivers trades within about 50 ms instead of about 1 second, and costs almost nothing against the rate limit. The catch is that it needs an authenticated, signed connection and a process running for the whole game.

Since minute-level matching only needs one price per minute, REST candles are enough for the core comparison. The WebSocket matters if we want to study fast moves, like the minutes right after a score.
